title: Fukanzazengi, Part 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett emphasizes that Dogen's teachings on zazen (meditation) are not about achieving a specific state through concentration or intellectual understanding, but rather about embracing the present moment with openness and acceptance. This approach encourages us to let go of our preconceptions and preferences, allowing us to experience our true nature as it is, unencumbered by thoughts and concepts. By turning our attention inward and letting go of distractions, we can access a deeper understanding of ourselves and the world around us, revealing our inherent interconnectedness and unity.

Another text in our chant book, one of a few that we have in there by Eihei Dogen, 1200 to 1252, the founder of our school of Japanese Zen, is a little meditation manual, a little manual on how to do zazen.

We kind of run it together, but you can hear zazen in the middle.
It means something like universal recommendation to do zazen.
This seems like a pretty sensible thing that a teacher would want to write down, right?
This is the most central thing in Zen, it seems, sitting.
At least that's the way Dogen talked about our practice.
To sit is central.
If you look at what we do here, it's a lot of what we do.
So you want to write a manual, but oddly it turns out this was not done.
Zen came from China, where the same character that the Japanese called Zen is called chan, but it's the same character.
In the chan tradition, they wrote a lot of stuff down.
They wrote down stories and biographies and sayings.
Any teacher worth his salt would end up with a collected sayings book.
So if you need something to do, I've got a lot of notes.
I don't seem to have time to write it though.
But there were actually no manuals about how to sit zazen.
There was almost nothing written.
There was a famous manual about how to conduct yourself at the monastery, which was a big part of things.
It was a monastic tradition.
Chan, originally, was not so much anybody's house, although the householders would come and visit the monks and support the monastery.
It was really done pretty exclusively by monks and nuns.
So there was a manual written about 600 about how to do the meals and how to go from this room, this building, to that building, and the routine of the day, and all the rules of the monastery.
It was a kind of extension of the precepts, put into action in the monastic life, which was a big emphasis in Zen.
They didn't do actually a whole lot of scholastic study.
The way to study Zen was to do Zen, not to study about Zen.
But even this manual from about 600 doesn't say much at all about zazen, just a few little notes in passing.
It's attributed to a teacher named Bai Zhong, Bai Zhong's monastic rules.
So it's not until the 11th century that we encounter a Chinese manual on zazen, by a teacher named Zongze.
Even that's pretty simple.
It describes the posture and how to arrange things and doesn't say much of anything about why you're doing it or what the point is.
It says how to do it.
Maybe all this was because it was oral instruction and oral tradition, whereas the sayings and doings of the great teachers had that kind of preciousness and they wanted to preserve them.
Everyone knew how to do this stuff.
We're always talking about that.
So maybe that's why they didn't write it down.
But around the 11th, 12th century in China and Japan, both, meditation started to trickle out a little bit more into the populace.
Not a lot, but a bit.
So maybe that's why they wanted to write things down.

It's also possible that these Zen leaders wanted to involve the aristocrats and the people with money and power in meditation so that they'd support the monastery more, because those are the people who could read.
That's possible too.
But anyway, just a little backstory.
Dogen had encountered this 11th century manual by the Chinese teacher Zongze.
After he got back from his adventure in China, where he went to study for four years, he wrote Fukanzazengi.
At least he wrote the first version of Fukanzazengi.
By then other people were doing this too, so he wasn't the only one, lest we think that.
A number of his contemporaries also wrote meditation manuals.
I thought that was kind of interesting.
But then it also gets a little bit tricky for us 800 years later to really know who wrote what, when, and what they intended.
Although there were printing presses using hand-carved wooden blocks, so that'd be a bit of work, huh?
They must have been few and far between and maybe only reserved for really important books.
So all of Dogen's work up until about the 18th century was handwritten.
Written originally by himself, and some things his student Ejo wrote down.
But then there would only be one copy, so if you want another copy, somebody has to copy it by hand.
These scrolls were precious, so they were tucked in special rooms in monasteries.
And sometimes they got lost in the back of the drawer for like a couple centuries.
Really, this would happen.
Then someone would get it out and start copying it, and then they'd say, well, that can't be what he meant.
That must be a mistake.
And change a little word or two.
They probably thought this couldn't be what Dogen meant, so the previous guy who copied it probably made a mistake, so I'm gonna fix it.
So the different versions tend to diverge over time.
Although we actually do have a copy of what we think is the earliest version of Fukanzazengi, probably, because it appears to be in Dogen's actual handwriting, which is rare.
There's only a few things actually in his hand that still exist.
It was mounted on really fancy paper and well preserved, so it was probably a gift for a patron who stuck it in a drawer for 600 years.
So it stayed in good shape.
Later another version of Fukanzazengi popped up, and it became the main version in like the 16th, 17th century, and it's a little bit different from when he wrote it originally, we think, maybe.
Or did he revise it?
We're not really sure.
So we have now our two main versions, one we believe to be early and one we believe to be late in Dogen's life.

There's a few places where they're different, so I thought we would do a little study of Fukanzazengi this week and next week, and when it seems interesting I'll highlight places where he changed it, or somebody changed it, probably Dogen.
If you're like me and you learn better if you can be looking, this is in the chant book.
Thanks, Marty.
We're just gonna look at the beginning of it.
Let's find out what page it's on.
Page 19.
You're welcome to just listen, or if it's easier for you to be reading and listening, please do.
Here's how he starts out this text, which I think he kind of meant to be a bit groundbreaking.

So I think he really thought, I'm gonna unleash something on the Japanese scene here.
And he wrote:
*The way is basically perfect and all-pervading.
How could it be contingent upon practice and realization?
The Dharma vehicle is free and untrammeled.
What need is there for concentrated effort?
Indeed, the whole body is far beyond the world's dust.

The way here means the teachings and also the true reality that the teachings point to.
The way, the way things are, the way of practice, the way of understanding, [unclear: "the way we always worry from the beginning but we got confused"].
The way, the deep way.

It's perfect and all-pervading.
How could it be contingent on something that we would do, called practice or even called realization?
So what do we have to do here?
What need is there for concentrated effort, he says.

Like, oh, relax.

Isn't that great, huh?

*Indeed, the whole body is far beyond the world's dust.
Who could believe in a means to brush it clean?* Body here means body and mind.

And then the second paragraph begins with a really pivotal clause.

Here you are.
Here we are.
